answer: Most likely cause: get_level() is called inside the for-loop, so the program asks 'Level:' before every one of the 10 problems. CS50's check50 script for Little Professor expects the level to be requested once at the very start of the run, then 10 arithmetic prompts. Because your program asks for a level 10 times instead of once, check50's scripted answers get misaligned after round 1 — an answer meant for 'X + Y =' gets consumed as a level, and eventually the program blocks on input() waiting for data check50 never sends, so check50 just sees the process hang and reports a timeout. Move the level prompt outside the loop so it's asked once. Also double-check indentation: print(f'Score: {score}') and sys.exit(0) should run unconditionally after the for-loop finishes, not only nested under the 'if errors == 3' branch, or check50 won't see the final score line when the last problem is answered correctly.

This isn't a pycryptodome bug. RSA.generate() computes the private exponent d as the modular inverse of e modulo Carmichael's function lambda(n) = lcm(p-1, q-1), not modulo Euler's totient phi(n) = (p-1)(q-1), following current best practice (FIPS 186-4). Since lambda(n) divides phi(n) and is strictly smaller whenever gcd(p-1, q-1) > 2, e*d = 1 (mod lambda(n)) does not imply e*d = 1 (mod phi(n)) in general — so your assert on f = (p-1)*(q-1) fails exactly when the generated p, q happen to have p-1 and q-1 share a larger common factor, which is why it looks 'random.' The key is still perfectly valid: encryption/decryption only require e*d = 1 mod lambda(n), which always holds. To make your check pass reliably, compute f as lcm(p-1, q-1) (gmpy2 has gm.lcm) instead of the plain product (p-1)*(q-1), and verify against that instead.

self.PetFrames is built once, at class-body execution time, using whatever State equals then (2 = 'Sad'), e.g. tk.PhotoImage(file=...+PetStates[State]+...). It's a class attribute, so it's evaluated exactly once when the class is defined/imported, not re-evaluated when you later change State. animation() only cycles self.frame between the two images already loaded into that fixed list — it never looks at State again to decide which images to load. So printing PetStates[State] correctly shows 'Idle' (the variable really did change), but canvas.itemconfig keeps showing frames from the original 'Sad' PhotoImage objects because those are the only images that were ever loaded. Fix: turn PetFrames construction into a method (e.g., load_frames()) that reads the current State/Pet and reloads the two PhotoImage objects, and call it every time State changes (or at the start of animation() if the state differs from what's currently loaded), instead of computing it once as a static class attribute.

Yes, a single collector could parse call syntax the same way Python already does (positional vs name=value), so ambiguity at the call site isn't really the blocker. The real reasons for keeping them separate: (1) Dict keys for kwargs must be valid identifier strings, while positional args have no such constraint — merging still needs two internal representations, so splitting them is just making that explicit rather than hiding it. (2) Separating them lets you declare only what you want to accept: def f(*args) rejects stray keywords, def f(**kwargs) rejects stray positionals, def f(*args, **kwargs) accepts both — a merged form couldn't express 'positional-only variadic' or 'keyword-only variadic' cleanly. (3) It enables keyword-only parameters after *args (def f(*args, key=None)) and forwarding idioms (def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): return f(*args, **kwargs)) that map directly onto how the callee itself binds arguments. (4) It matches Python's general binding model and keeps introspection (inspect.signature) unambiguous. It's about explicitness and expressiveness, not avoiding parser ambiguity.

atexit callbacks run late in interpreter shutdown, and on Windows that timing is fragile — by the time console_pause fires, streams can already be in a half-torn-down state, especially under a batch file where stdin/stdout handles are set up differently than an interactive console launched from Explorer. Given your output shows several file writes before the pause, if any of that involves multiprocessing/joblib-style worker processes, note that on Windows child processes re-import your main module; if that ever re-triggers the same atexit call in a worker whose stdio isn't a real console, you'd get exactly this 'I/O operation on closed file' on the second occurrence. Rather than fighting atexit's shutdown-order guarantees, don't use atexit for an interactive pause: call console_pause explicitly yourself at the true end of your program (e.g., in a try/finally wrapped around your real entry-point logic), so it runs exactly once, in the main process, before any teardown starts. Also wrap the input() call itself in try/except (ValueError, OSError) to silently ignore this specific harmless failure.

This is a real quirk/inconsistency in np.vectorize, not documented guaranteed behavior. Without otypes, vectorize first makes a 'trial call' on one extracted element (via .flat[0]) purely to infer the output dtype — that trial call overflows (hence the warning), but its numeric result is discarded once otypes=float64 is decided; it isn't reused for the real computation. The actual elementwise pass afterward goes through a different internal path once the target dtype is known, which for your single-element input happens to avoid the overflow, giving -40. When you pass otypes explicitly, vectorize skips the trial call entirely and just wraps your function via frompyfunc, calling it on each element with its original uint8 dtype every time, faithfully reproducing the overflowing 216. So the discrepancy comes from the trial-call and real-call paths handling dtype differently — closer to an implementation inconsistency than intended design. Since np.vectorize is only a convenience loop, not actually vectorized/fast, safest is to cast x to float before subtracting rather than depend on its dtype-inference behavior.

Python's stdlib uuid module has an optional C accelerator, the _uuid extension module (uuid.py does a bare 'try: import _uuid' internally). PyInstaller's static import scanner doesn't reliably detect this internal, lazily-imported C extension, so it isn't bundled even when you hidden-import uuid itself. psycopg (3)'s UUID type adapter constructs uuid.UUID objects when parsing returned rows, which triggers that internal import at SELECT time; INSERT only serializes an existing Python value to text and never hits that code path, which is why only SELECT breaks. Fix: explicitly add _uuid (not just uuid) as a hidden import: pyinstaller --onefile --hidden-import=uuid --hidden-import=_uuid __main__.py. If that alone doesn't work, also try --collect-submodules=uuid, or manually copy the _uuid*.pyd from your Python installation's DLLs folder next to the built exe, and make sure your PyInstaller version is current for your Python version, since bundling support for this particular internal extension has changed across PyInstaller releases.

That's expected: @mcp.resource with a URI containing a placeholder like greeting://{name} registers a resource TEMPLATE, not a static resource. The MCP spec exposes these through a separate capability/endpoint (resources/templates/list) from plain resources/list, precisely because a templated URI isn't directly readable — a client would need to supply a value for {name} first. file://data/file.txt has no placeholder, so it's a concrete resource and shows up in the normal resources list; get_greeting doesn't, because it's only enumerable via the templates listing. Many clients/tools, including Claude Desktop and some versions of the MCP inspector, only surface plain resources in their UI and don't yet have a picker for templated ones (they can't prompt the user for the {name} value), so it silently looks 'missing' rather than erroring. Nothing is wrong with your code. If you need it usable from a client without template support, either call resources/templates/list directly against your server to confirm it's registered, or expose the same functionality as a @mcp.tool() instead, since tools take arguments naturally.

Exit code -1073741819 (0xC0000005) is a raw Windows access-violation crash at the native/C level — Python itself never gets a chance to raise a catchable exception, which is why firewall/port changes don't help; the process dies before it even opens a socket. This is a known issue with mysql-connector-python's C extension on Windows, usually from a DLL mismatch or conflict: wrong architecture (32 vs 64-bit) between Python and the connector build, or duplicate OpenSSL/libcrypto DLLs on PATH (very common if you also have Anaconda, MySQL Server, or other tools that ship their own copies). Two quick fixes: 1) force the pure-Python implementation to sidestep the C extension entirely: mysql.connector.connect(..., use_pure=True); 2) fully reinstall the connector: pip uninstall mysql-connector-python, then pip install mysql-connector-python --no-cache-dir, ideally in a clean virtualenv matching your Python's bitness. Also make sure no local file is named mysql.py shadowing the package, and that you don't have both mysql-connector and mysql-connector-python installed simultaneously.

Yes, this is a legitimate and fairly common pattern — build() is the standard place to defer any construction that depends on input_shape, and that includes instantiating sub-layers, not just calling self.add_weight directly. Keras tracks any Layer assigned as an attribute on self automatically, so weights of res_conv/res_norm created in build() are still discovered, trained, and (de)serialized correctly as long as construction is deterministic given input_shape. A few real pitfalls to watch: 1) build() is normally called only once per layer instance — if the same instance could ever see a different input_shape later, guard re-creation (e.g., if self.res_conv is None) or it'll silently reuse stale sub-layers. 2) Always call super().build(input_shape) (or ensure self.built = True) at the end, which you're doing. 3) Sub-layers created in build() still get their own build() triggered automatically the first time you call them in call(), so you don't need to build them manually. 4) Keep attributes needed inside build() (out_channels, stride) set in __init__ before build() ever runs. Overall, your implementation is fine.

st.dataframe and st.data_editor render through Streamlit's own interactive grid component, which does not respect pandas Styler CSS for the header row — Styler support in Streamlit is limited to certain cell-level formatting, and there's no parameter to color the header at all in either function. Practical options: 1) Switch to st.table, which renders a static (non-interactive, non-scrolling) HTML table and honors much more of pandas Styler, including header styling via Styler.set_table_styles() targeting the 'th' selector or applymap_index. 2) For full control while keeping it visual, bypass Streamlit's table widgets entirely and render your own HTML: st.markdown(df.style.set_table_styles([{'selector': 'th', 'props': [('background-color', 'blue')]}]).to_html(), unsafe_allow_html=True). You lose st.dataframe's sorting/scrolling/interactivity this way. 3) Global theme colors (config.toml [theme] section) affect the whole app's look but not per-column header colors. There is currently no supported way to color individual st.dataframe header cells directly.

There's no fixed maximum where a Python set stops being O(1) — CPython's set/dict implementation automatically resizes its underlying hash table as you add elements, keeping the load factor low, so membership testing ('in') stays average-case O(1) regardless of how many elements are in it (amortized, not size-dependent). The only real limits are practical, not algorithmic: 1) available RAM — each element costs roughly 100+ bytes once you include the hash table slot overhead and the referenced object itself, so a set of 10^9 elements can need tens of gigabytes; 2) the theoretical container-size ceiling tied to sys.maxsize, far beyond anything reachable by memory anyway. Worst-case lookup degrades toward O(n) only under pathological hash collisions, which Python's hashing is designed to avoid for normal data. So: it scales to however many elements fit in memory while keeping O(1) average lookup throughout — there isn't a size threshold after which it stops being 'constant time.'

A general, efficient approach: instead of pairwise comparisons (O(n^2)), map every list to a canonical representative under the symmetry group and dedupe with a set (O(n*|G|)). Represent the graph's automorphism group as a list of index-permutations, then take, for each el, the lexicographically smallest tuple among [tuple(el[i] for i in perm) for perm in group] as its canonical form; keep el only if that canonical form hasn't been seen before (store seen forms in a set). For your D4 example, since a,b,d,e are all leaves attached only to the center c, ANY permutation of positions {0,1,3,4} is a graph automorphism, so build group from itertools.permutations over those four positions (position 2 always fixed) rather than hand-coding the reflection case. This generalizes to any graph: compute its automorphism group once (by hand for small cases, or with networkx/pynauty/sympy for larger ones), then reuse the same canonical-form dedup logic regardless of how complex the symmetry is.

Two separate issues. First, a plain dbus-monitor --session with no filter often won't show another app's method calls unless you add an explicit match rule, since eavesdropping is restricted by default on modern dbus: try dbus-monitor --session "interface='org.freedesktop.Notifications',member='Notify'" and you should see the app_name, summary, and body arguments printed for every notification. Second, your Python script isn't seeing anything because org.freedesktop.Notifications on a normal Ubuntu/GNOME session is already owned by gnome-shell/mutter (the real notification daemon) — you can't also register your own service under that same well-known bus name; any attempt to 'implement' it yourself will just fail to receive calls meant for the real daemon. What you actually want is a passive eavesdropper/monitor, not a competing implementation: use dbus-monitor as above (simplest), or in dbus_next, add an explicit match rule with eavesdrop=true on the MessageBus and filter member=='Notify', rather than trying to export your own object at that path.

x-tagGroups is actually a ReDoc-specific vendor extension (not part of core OpenAPI, and Swagger UI itself ignores it), and flask-restx has no built-in hook to add arbitrary top-level extensions like that to the generated spec — its vendor() decorator only lets you attach x- extensions at the operation level, not the document level. The practical workaround is to post-process the generated schema yourself: flask-restx builds and caches the full OpenAPI dict on the Api instance (accessible as api.__schema__), so you can override the /swagger.json route to fetch that dict, inject 'x-tagGroups': [...] into it, and return the modified JSON instead of the default one — e.g. disable the built-in doc route and add your own that does: spec = api.__schema__; spec['x-tagGroups'] = [...]; return jsonify(spec). That gives you full control over top-level spec keys without needing library support, and you can combine it with your existing per-operation vendor({'x-internal-endpoint': 'true'}) tags to decide which operations to filter or group before serving the doc to external consumers.

Classic Flask session gotcha: session is a MutableMapping backed by a signed cookie, and Flask only knows to re-sign/re-send an updated cookie when it detects a change — by default that means a direct assignment to a top-level key (session['x'] = ...). del session['cart'][item_index] mutates the list object stored inside the session in place; Flask's session wrapper doesn't inspect nested containers, so it never marks itself modified, and the response goes out with the old cookie unchanged. That's why your prints inside remove_item show the correct shrunk list (you really did mutate it in memory for that request), but the next request's session — rebuilt fresh from the client's still-old cookie — is back to 3 items. Fix: after mutating a nested structure, explicitly set session.modified = True before returning/redirecting, right after the del call. Alternatively, reassign the whole list back to the key (cart = session['cart']; del cart[item_index]; session['cart'] = cart), since a direct top-level assignment triggers the modified flag automatically.

Your current approach already compiles to a single SQL query with a subquery (as long as assigned_objects stays a lazy QuerySet and you never call list()/evaluate it early), so it's not actually hitting the DB twice — that part is fine as written. A cleaner and often more efficient alternative is to skip building an id list entirely and filter directly through the reverse OneToOne relation: CartObject.objects.filter(status='pending', associated_process__isnull=True).order_by('-id'). This compiles to a single LEFT JOIN with associated_process_id IS NULL instead of a NOT IN (subquery), which is typically easier for the query planner to optimize and sidesteps the classic SQL gotcha where NOT IN behaves surprisingly if the subquery could ever return a NULL. It's also more idiomatic Django — you're expressing 'has no related OnGoingProcess' directly rather than manually excluding by id. Add a DB index on OnGoingProcess.associated_object (Django already creates one for OneToOneField) and on CartObject.status if this table is large; this scales well without extra Python-side filtering.

This is a bug in the Flake8 VS Code extension itself (tracked upstream as you found), where it's passing a raw format string to flake8's reporter factory as if it were a registered format name, so reporters[format_name] raises KeyError instead of falling back to the default reporter. Two workarounds while it's unfixed: 1) Check your user and workspace settings.json for any leftover flake8.args or output-format-related setting (e.g., a --format=... entry) and remove it so the extension falls back to its built-in default reporter instead of trying to look up a custom format string as a name. 2) If nothing like that is set, roll back to a previously working extension version: in the Extensions panel, find Flake8, click the gear icon, choose 'Install Another Version…', and pick the release before 2026.4.0. As a last resort, disable the extension and run flake8 from an integrated terminal or a VS Code task instead of relying on the inline linter until the upstream fix (issues 501/503) lands.

First check your SQLAlchemy version: 2.0+ already batches same-table INSERTs from a single flush into one real multi-row INSERT ... VALUES (...),(...),(...) via the 'insertmanyvalues' feature (on Postgres/SQLite/MySQL), even for ORM-cascaded child objects — turn on echo=True and check whether you're already getting one statement per table before doing anything else. If you're on 1.4, or insertmanyvalues isn't kicking in for your dialect, there's no supported public hook to intercept and merge the unit-of-work's per-instance INSERTs while keeping cascade='all' semantics intact — the ORM issues them one row at a time by design, specifically so it can retrieve each generated primary key before flushing dependent rows that reference it via FK. The practical workaround is to give up ORM cascade for the bulk step: after building cfg.trans/cfg.scripts in Python, pre-assign or reserve primary keys yourself and insert each child table directly with session.execute(insert(Trans), [dict(...), ...]), bypassing autoflush/cascade for those tables while still using the ORM for cfg itself.

SQLAlchemy filter expressions like User.age > 28 build a SQL ClauseElement meant to be compiled into SQL — there's no built-in way to evaluate that same expression object against a plain in-memory instance without going back to the database; SQLAlchemy isn't an in-memory rules/expression engine. For a simple case like this, the practical answer is to just re-check the equivalent plain Python condition directly: u2.age > 28. If you want to avoid duplicating logic, define the condition once as a reusable predicate and use it both ways, e.g. a small helper is_match(age) that returns age > 28, used for the in-memory check, while the query keeps its own equivalent filter — there's no automatic way to derive one from the other. For genuinely complex, multi-clause filters there's no first-party SQLAlchemy feature to 'compile down' a Query/select() into a reusable Python predicate callable; you'd have to hand-maintain parallel logic or look outside SQLAlchemy for an expression-evaluation library that can inspect the clause tree and evaluate it against attribute access.
